name: Ligament Crucible
description: Ligament Crucible is a small, furious world held together by geological forces that seem to exceed what its mass should produce. Chains of volcanoes link the surface in connected arcs, their eruptions synchronized in patterns that suggest deep structural connections binding the planet's fractured crust. An orbital debris ring of shattered moonlets circles the equator, raining fragments onto the surface in periodic meteor showers that trigger fresh eruptions.

The toxic atmosphere glows a sickly amber from below, lit by the constant volcanic activity, and from above by the burning debris ring. The low gravity means eruptions send material high enough to interact with the ring, creating a cycle of destruction and reformation that has persisted for millions of years. The sound on the surface is a grinding, tearing cacophony, as though the world is constantly pulling itself apart and stitching itself back together.

A graveyard of satellites and probes orbits within the debris ring, their missions ended by the constant bombardment of volcanic ejecta and ring fragments. The synchronized eruption patterns have defied explanation, behaving less like independent geological events and more like the coordinated contractions of a single system. Early surveys classified the planet as unremarkable; that assessment has been repeatedly revised upward.

The debris ring contains fragments of the original moonlets that show unusual mineral compositions worth investigating, but navigation through the ring is treacherous at best. The synchronized eruptions have begun to change their pattern, accelerating over the past century in a trend that suggests the planet is approaching some kind of geological tipping point. Whether Ligament Crucible will tear itself apart or reach a new equilibrium remains the subject of considerable scientific debate and significant wagers.
